summary: Provides guidelines and recommendations for defining new URI schemes, and updates the process and IANA registry for them. It obsoletes RFC 2717 and RFC 2718. It is a Best Current Practice and was replaced by RFC 7595.

eli5.summary: Rules for inventing a new kind of web address prefix, like http: or mailto:, and for getting it written in the official list.

questions: how to register a new uri scheme
subtitle: How to design and register new web address prefixes

tldr.problem: The IETF had no clear process for designing new URI schemes (like http:, mailto:, ftp:), and the two previous RFCs on the topic distinguished between URLs and URNs in ways that became impractical to apply.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4395 establishes clear guidelines for defining a URI scheme (demonstrable utility, syntactic compatibility, clear security analysis) and a single registry with two categories: permanent (meeting all criteria) and provisional (lower bar for experimentation).
tldr.outcome: This BCP established a standardized process that replaced RFC 2717/2718 and remained in use until RFC 7595 updated the registration procedures further.

facts.value: 8 (utility, syntax, definitions, operations, context, encoding, security, scheme name)

facts.value: 4 weeks recommended for mailing list discussion

today: RFC 4395 is a Best Current Practice that was replaced by RFC 7595 in June 2015, which updated the registration procedures while maintaining the same philosophy of clear guidelines and a tiered registry.

sections.title: URI Schemes and the Problem
sections.content:
A Uniform Resource Identifier (URI) is any web address that starts with a scheme name. The scheme name (such as http, ftp, mailto) tells software how to handle what comes next. RFC 3986 defined the generic URI syntax, but left room for new schemes.

Before RFC 4395, two older RFCs (2717 and 2718) tried to distinguish between URLs (locators, for accessing resources) and URNs (names, for identifying abstract things). This distinction proved hard to apply in practice: locators can act as names, and names can act as locators. The practical lesson: using the umbrella term URI for all resource identifiers, and registering schemes that have clear utility, is simpler than trying to categorize them.
sections.eli5: A URI is any address like http://example.com. The first word (http) is the scheme. Old rules tried to separate address-like and name-like URIs, but it did not work well. New rules just ask: does it have real use, and is it defined clearly?

sections.title: Guidelines for Permanent URI Schemes
sections.content:
To register a scheme permanently, it must meet these criteria:

Demonstrable, new, long-lived utility. Adding a new URI scheme costs money: software, gateways, proxies, and caches must all be updated. The scheme must serve a need the Internet community has, beyond what existing schemes already do.

Syntactic compatibility. Every URI scheme must follow the generic syntax rules in RFC 3986. Schemes that use a hierarchical structure should reuse the common URI components (like the forward slash for hierarchy). Schemes should avoid double slashes unless they define a hierarchical structure. Reserved characters must be clearly defined, showing which are delimiters and which must be escaped.

Well-defined. A scheme definition must clearly explain how the resource is identified or accessed. If the scheme translates another namespace (like FTP) into URIs, both mappings must be complete: from URI to FTP action, and from FTP actions to valid URIs. Binary or character encoding must be specified.

Definition of operations. The scheme must define what operations apply to its URIs (like HTTP's GET, POST, PUT). It is acceptable to say "only GET applies" or "no GET-like operations apply"; the important point is describing what is defined.

Context of use. If a scheme is intended for specific protocols or applications, the definition should identify them and provide references.

Internationalization and character encoding. If text appears in URIs, the scheme must specify how characters are encoded and how the scheme interacts with Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs).

Clear security considerations. Every scheme definition must include a security analysis, noting which of the general security considerations from RFC 3986 apply to the specific scheme.

Scheme name considerations. Scheme names must be lowercase, short yet descriptive, and avoid trademark or trademark-like names. Avoid overly general names or names the community associates with other protocols.
sections.eli5: A permanent scheme needs to prove it is useful and not just a copy of something that exists. It must follow the address rules everyone knows, define what operations it supports, explain how text is encoded, and describe safety concerns. It should have a clear, short name.

sections.title: Provisional, Permanent, and Historical Registration
sections.content:
The RFC establishes three categories in the registry:

Permanent registration requires meeting all guidelines in Section 2. These are schemes the IETF community endorses as well-designed and broadly useful.

Provisional registration has a lower bar: the scheme name must be syntactically valid, unique in the registry, and include contact information. A permanent specification or credible reasons for not having one are needed. The scheme must include a valid Security Considerations section and note any ways it deviates from the guidelines. This category encourages registration of schemes in actual use, even if they don't yet meet the full guidelines.

Historical registration marks schemes that were once registered or in use but are no longer common. Anyone can request a scheme be registered as historical, which preserves its history and prevents reuse of the name.
sections.eli5: There are three slots in the registry: permanent (if you do it right), provisional (if you want to try something new), and historical (if it is old and not used anymore).

sections.title: Registration Process
sections.content:
A person wanting to register a scheme should:

1. Check the IANA registry to ensure the name is not already used.

2. Prepare a registration template including the scheme name, status (permanent, provisional, or historical), syntax, semantics, encoding considerations, applications, interoperability notes, security considerations, contact information, author/change controller, and references.

3. Submit the template to the uri-review@ietf.org mailing list for discussion, plus any other relevant mailing lists. Allow four weeks for permanent registrations.

4. Respond to comments and revise as needed.

5. Submit the final template to IANA, specifying the desired status.

Upon receipt, IANA checks for completeness and uniqueness, then requests Expert Review. The Designated Expert evaluates against the criteria for the requested status. If Expert Review recommends registration, IANA adds it. If no explicit rejection occurs within two weeks, IANA should automatically add a provisional registration.

Provisional registrations can be updated by the original registrant, and the IESG can reassign responsibility if the original registrant is unreachable. Upgrading from provisional to permanent follows the same process as initial permanent registration; promoting historical status requires IESG approval.
sections.eli5: To register a scheme: check if the name is free, write down the rules, ask the community for feedback for a few weeks, then send it to IANA. They check it and ask an expert to review it. If the expert says yes, your scheme goes in the list.

sections.title: Security and Special Cases
sections.content:
All registered schemes must include accurate security sections. Security properties can change as new vulnerabilities emerge, so documentation may need to be updated.

The RFC clarifies the handling of private namespaces: organizations wanting a private URI scheme should use a prefix based on their domain name in reverse order (for example, com-example-info for example.com).

The registration process also accommodates Internationalized Resource Identifiers (IRIs), defined in RFC 3987. There is no separate IRI registry; those who want to describe resource identifiers useful as IRIs should define the URI syntax and note that IRI usage follows RFC 3987's rules.
sections.eli5: Security can change as hackers get smarter, so documentation for a scheme can be updated. Organizations can claim their own private schemes using a reverse domain prefix. International domain names follow separate rules.
